headline: Threadit Community Proposes: What If 5G Towers Are Actually Just Very Tall Birds?
subheadline: Post reaches 847K upvotes as users note towers 'have never been seen moving'
summary: A Threadit theory suggests 5G infrastructure may be elaborate camouflage for large avian entities standing very still.
content:
What started as a joke post on r/conspiracytheory has evolved into what adherents call "the only theory that explains everything."

User u/TowerBirdTruther posted a simple observation three weeks ago: "5G towers have the same silhouette as herons. They're always near roads, like birds hunting for roadkill. And crucially: has anyone ever seen one being built? Or do they just... appear?"

The post now has 847,000 upvotes and has spawned a dedicated subreddit with 23,000 members.

"Think about it," explained moderator u/StillStanding_Watcher in a viral follow-up post. "Cell towers don't move. Neither do birds when they're hunting. The 5G signals? That's echolocation. They're mapping us. Not for the government. For migration."

The theory has developed elaborate lore. According to believers, the towers are a species called "Infrastructicus Giganticus" that evolved to mimic human technology. The blinking red lights are eyes. The signals are calls to each other, coordinating something adherents simply call "The Flyover."

"I drove past the same tower for three years," reported one convert. "Last Tuesday, it was on the other side of the highway. No one else noticed. No construction. It just moved. During the night. Like it was roosting somewhere else."

Telecommunications companies have declined to comment, though one anonymous industry insider told reporters: "This is the first conspiracy theory about us that I genuinely wish was true. It would explain so much about our infrastructure maintenance."

Dr. Elena Martinez of the local university physics department, when asked for comment, replied: "I'm not touching this one. I've learned my lesson about lending scientific credibility to internet theories." She did not elaborate.

The community has begun tracking tower "sightings" on a shared Gooble map. At press time, 847 towers had been flagged as "suspicious" based on criteria including "too perfect posture," "facing the wind," and "looks like it's waiting for something."
author: Alex Rivera, Digital Culture
